Recursion is a programming technique where a function calls itself to solve a problem, breaking the problem into smaller, similar sub‑problems. The function must have a **base case**—a simple condition that stops the recursion—to avoid calling itself forever. Each recursive call works on a reduced version of the original input, and when the base case is reached, the results are combined as the calls unwind back up the call stack. Think of it like a set of nested Russian dolls: you keep opening a doll (making a recursive call) until you reach the smallest one (the base case), then you close them back together.
